title: How The Voynich Manuscript Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Voynich Manuscript, a fifteenth-century illustrated codex written in an undeciphered script. They cover its provenance from Rudolph II and Jacobus Typotius through Georg Baresch, Jan Marci, Athanasius Kircher, and Wilfrid Voynich, to Yale. They describe the book's physical features and illustrations, the failed codebreaking attempts (including William and Elizabeth Friedman), and theories ranging from hoax and gibberish to a lost language, mental illness, religious glossolalia, and drug-induced creation. They discuss statistical analyses (Zipf's law, word patterns) and recent claimed decipherments by Stephen Bax and Nick Pelling, and the Alpine/northern Italian origin theories. The episode closes with listener mail about a baby who falls asleep to the show.

segments.title: Opening banter and Berenstain Bears aside
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode and describe the Voynich Manuscript as a medieval codex in an unreadable script with unusual plant and figure illustrations. They joke about the Berenstain/Berenstein Bears Mandela effect and float their own theories.

segments.title: Provenance: Rudolph II to Baresch and Kircher
segments.summary: The manuscript is traced to Emperor Rudolph II, who reportedly paid 600 ducats for it and believed it was Roger Bacon's work. It was later owned by Georg Baresch, who sent it to Athanasius Kircher, and was passed to Jan Marci. A court pharmacist, Jacobus Typotius, had a faint mark in it, supporting Rudolph's ownership.

segments.title: Sponsor break: The Message podcast
segments.summary: Ad read promoting the podcast series The Message from iHeart/Panoply.

segments.title: Wilfrid Voynich and early codebreaking attempts
segments.summary: Wilfrid Voynich bought the manuscript and tried hard to crack it, which gave it his name. Early attempts included a University of Pennsylvania philosopher who claimed microscopic figures in the ink encoded Greek letters and a Roger Bacon message; this was rejected. Then William and Elizabeth Friedman and colleagues tried after World War II and gave up after about thirty years.

segments.title: Physical description, illustrations and structure
segments.summary: The manuscript has about 246 pages (possibly missing up to 55), is on calfskin, measures about nine by six inches, and is written left to right in roughly thirty to forty characters with no punctuation. It contains about 220 illustrations in six apparent sections: botanical, astronomical, biological (including women in water-like settings), cosmological, pharmaceutical, and recipes. Word repetition and word-length patterns are noted.

segments.title: Sponsor break
segments.summary: Brief ad break before the discussion resumes.

segments.title: Hoax, gibberish and other theories
segments.summary: The hosts review theories: a hoax or gibberish, an unknown real language, an intentionally impenetrable cipher, mental illness, religious glossolalia, and the hosts' joking drug-induced theories. Statistical analysis finds patterns like Zipf's law that resemble natural language, which argues against a simple hoax, though hoax supporters note Renaissance forgeries existed.

segments.title: Recent decipherment claims and origin theories
segments.summary: Stephen Bax at the University of Bedfordshire claims to have identified about fourteen characters by matching plant and constellation illustrations to names. Nick Pelling proposed an Italian architect named Antonio Averlino as author, which has been disputed. Alpine and northern Italian origins are discussed, and Rene Zandbergen's website is recommended.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts close, pointing to the website and the Yale library, and sign off.
